canonical_claim: The notes list endpoint (GET /api/notes/:postcode) produces non-deterministic ordering when tests run concurrently because the in-memory Map accumulates state across parallel test runners — this same shared-state design means production concurrent requests can also observe inconsistent or interleaved note lists.

absorbed.claim: Notes have implicit temporal/ordering metadata: the list endpoint returns notes 'in insertion order', but the in-memory Map storage is non-deterministic under concurrent test runners, meaning insertion-order guarantees are a data-integrity concern that is already producing test instability.

The in-memory Map storage causes non-deterministic test ordering when test suites run in parallel, because note state accumulates across concurrent test runners — a symptom that also manifests under concurrent load in production.

The notes list endpoint (GET /api/notes/:postcode) may return results in non-deterministic order under concurrent load because the shared in-memory Map accumulates state across parallel callers with no synchronisation, as already observed in the test suite.

The notesRoutes test 'should list all notes for a postcode (returns in insertion order)' is at-risk of flakiness because the shared in-memory Map accumulates state across parallel test runners, producing non-deterministic ordering. This makes the test suite unreliable for CI gating.

canonical_claim: There is no ownership or session scoping on PUT and DELETE /api/notes/:id; any client that knows or guesses a note ID can modify or delete notes created by a different client session, making notes incompatible with any multi-user or shared-environment deployment.

absorbed.claim: A malicious or curious user who knows or can guess a note's ID can modify or delete notes created by any other user/session, because PUT and DELETE /api/notes/:id have no ownership verification.

PUT /api/notes/:id and DELETE /api/notes/:id accept any note ID with no ownership verification — a client that knows or guesses another session's note ID can modify or delete that note without authorization.

canonical_claim: The notes service stores all data in a bare in-memory Map with no persistence abstraction, meaning a server restart destroys all user notes and there is no interface to swap in a real database without rewriting the service layer.

absorbed.claim: All notes data is lost on server restart because the notes store is a bare in-memory Map with no persistence; any notes created before a restart will not be present after it.
All notes data is permanently lost on every server restart because the notes store is an in-memory Map with no persistence layer — there is no database, file, or external store backing it.

canonical_claim: The notes service stores all notes in a bare in-memory Map with no cap on the total number of notes per postcode; under sustained use, this accumulates unboundedly in heap memory and can cause an OOM crash that affects all features sharing the same server process.

absorbed.claim: The notes storage backend has no cap on the total number of notes per postcode; sustained use will accumulate notes unboundedly in heap memory, eventually causing an OOM crash that affects all features system-wide.

Sustained creation of notes (without deletions) causes unbounded heap growth in the server process because the in-memory Map has no per-postcode or global note count cap, which can eventually crash the server and affect all features.
